01.note: Binyamin the righteous ran the community charity fund. In a year of drought a woman begged him to support her; he swore there was nothing left in the fund, and she answered that without help she and her seven sons would die. So he supported her from his own money. Later he fell deathly ill, and the ministering angels argued before God that a man who had saved a woman and seven children should not die so young. His sentence was torn up at once, and a Sage taught that twenty-two years were added to his life. A second tale follows: King Munbaz gave away his own and his ancestors' treasures in years of drought, and when his family protested, he answered with a string of verses that his ancestors stored treasure below, on earth, while he stored it above, in heaven.
01.why: The Gemara has just told how Rava gave a Persian queen's gift to the gentile poor, in the middle of a discussion of charity; these two tales continue that theme by praising those who give generously in hard times, before the Gemara returns to the mishna's rules on town residents.

people.name: Binyamin the righteous
people.about: The man in charge of the charity fund, who fed a starving woman and her seven sons from his own money.

people.name: King Munbaz
people.about: A king who gave away his family's treasures to the poor during years of drought.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code, but is quoted in the Gemara.
The angels who serve God in heaven; here they plead with God on Binyamin's behalf.
The life after this one, in which, in rabbinic thought, a person is rewarded for good deeds.

01.flag: The STORY joins two separate tales, Binyamin the righteous and King Munbaz.

02.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi was standing in the street of Mehoza when he heard a fool announce that the next head of the yeshiva in Mata Mehasya would be a man who signs his name Tavyumei. Since he was the only Sage who signed that way, he took it as a sign his time had come and set off for Mata Mehasya. By the time he arrived, the Sages had already decided to appoint Rav Aha of Difti. When they heard he had come, they sent pairs of Sages to consult him, and he kept each pair with him until there were ten; then he began to teach and lecture, and was appointed. Rav Aha applied to himself the saying that one who is treated badly will not soon be treated well, and one who is treated well will not soon be treated badly.
02.why: The Gemara is discussing whether prophecy survives among the Sages; Rabbi Yohanan says that after the Temple fell it passed to fools and children, and this incident is the Gemara's example of a fool's words coming true.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who signed his name Tavyumei and took a fool's words as a sign he would head the yeshiva.

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: The Sage the others had chosen as head of the yeshiva before Mar bar Rav Ashi arrived.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who says prophecy was given to fools and children after the Temple was destroyed.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study; its head was its chief teacher and authority.
Large public study gatherings held in the months of Elul and Adar; the text says a lecture there may not open with fewer than ten men present.

03.note: Rav Hisda's young daughter was sitting on her father's lap while two Sages, Rava and Rami bar Hama, sat before him. Rav Hisda asked her which of the two she would like. She answered: both of them. Rava then said: and I will be last. The translation adds that this came true: she married Rami bar Hama first and, after he died, Rava.
03.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yohanan that after the Temple was destroyed prophecy was given to fools and children; having shown a fool's words coming true, it now gives this as its example of a child's.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who jokingly asks his small daughter which of his two students she wants.

people.name: Rava
people.about: One of the two Sages sitting before Rav Hisda; he says he will be her last husband.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The other Sage sitting before Rav Hisda.

04.note: Rav Huna wrote seventy Torah scrolls himself, and only once did one come out with its height exactly equal to its rolled-up circumference. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov wrote a single scroll, on calf hide, and it came out right. The Sages looked at him, and he died.
04.why: The Gemara has just taught that a Torah scroll should be as tall as it is round when rolled, and that even Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not know the right size for parchment; these reports show how rarely anyone managed it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who wrote seventy Torah scrolls and got the proportions exactly right only once.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
people.about: A Sage who wrote one Torah scroll on calf hide that came out exactly right, and then died when the Sages looked at him.

terms.meaning: A handwritten parchment scroll of the Five Books of Moses, rolled on poles and read in the synagogue.
The translation explains this as a jealous gaze, the evil eye, which the text treats as the cause of his death.

05.note: A daughter was born to Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and he was upset. His father comforted him: through daughters, increase comes into the world. Bar Kappara told Rabbi Shimon that this was empty comfort, and quoted a teaching: the world cannot exist without males and females, yet fortunate is the one whose children are sons and woe to the one whose children are daughters, just as the world needs both a spice seller and a tanner, but fortunate is the spice seller and woe to the tanner.
05.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish have just disagreed whether the birth of daughters brought increase or strife into the world; this exchange plays out the same disagreement in a real family, and the Gemara next links it to a dispute over whether Abraham had a daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; upset when a daughter is born to him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's father, who tells him that daughters bring increase into the world.

people.name: Bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage who tells Rabbi Shimon that his father's comfort was empty.

terms.meaning: A worker who turns animal hides into leather, a notoriously foul-smelling trade, set against the sweet-smelling spice seller.
A teaching from the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the core law code, but quoted in the Gemara.

06.note: Rav Dimi of Neharde'a brought a ship of dried figs to sell. The Exilarch told Rava to see whether he was a Torah scholar, and if so to reserve the market for him. Rava sent his student Rav Adda bar Abba, who asked a hard question about an elephant that swallowed a basket and passed it whole. Rav Dimi could not answer; Rav Adda struck him on his shoe and said he was his teacher, and Rava his teacher's teacher. The market was not reserved and the figs were lost. Rav Dimi complained to Rav Yosef, who called for punishment of whoever shamed him. Rav Adda bar Abba died, and five Sages each said, I punished him. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak, kept waiting that day, said he was waiting for Rav Adda's bier, and word came that he had died; the Gemara says his words most likely caused it.
06.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a town may keep outside merchants from setting up shop, but that a Torah scholar is an exception; this story shows the Exilarch applying that exception by checking whether a visiting merchant is really a scholar.

people.name: Rav Dimi of Neharde'a
people.about: A Sage who came to sell dried figs and lost them after failing Rav Adda bar Abba's test.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Abba
people.about: Rava's student, sent to test Rav Dimi; he shamed him and later died.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage the Exilarch asks to check Rav Dimi; he also says he caused Rav Adda's death.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage Rav Dimi complains to; he says he cursed Rav Adda bar Abba.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: Head of the kalla lectures, who reviewed his lesson daily with Rav Adda and announced he was waiting for his bier.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a leader with official standing.
To give one seller the exclusive right to sell his goods, so no one competes with him until they are sold.
An expression meaning to test someone and find out what he knows.
Large public study gatherings held in the months of Elul and Adar.

07.note: Rav Yosef owned some small palm trees. Bloodletters used to sit under them to work, and crows came to eat the blood, then flew up into the trees and damaged the dates. Rav Yosef told the bloodletters to take their crows away. Abaye objected that the damage was only indirect, and that they had a long-standing right to that spot. Rav Yosef answered with rulings of other Sages: indirect damage is forbidden, and no long-standing right can be held to cause damage. When Abaye said that rule was stated only for smoke and a bathroom, Rav Yosef replied that he was sensitive, and to him this was just like smoke and a bathroom.
07.why: Rav Tovi bar Mattana has just concluded from the mishna on ladders and dovecotes that causing even indirect damage is forbidden; here Rav Yosef applies that very ruling to his own trees.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage whose palm trees were damaged because of the bloodletters working beneath them.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who challenges his demand that the bloodletters leave.

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Mattana
people.about: A Sage whose ruling that indirect damage is forbidden Rav Yosef quotes.

terms.meaning: A practitioner who drew blood from people as a medical treatment, a common remedy at the time.
Damage a person does not do himself but sets in motion, as when the bloodletters' work draws crows that ruin the dates.
A right to keep using something in a certain way because it has gone on unchallenged for a long time.

08.note: Pappei Yona'a had been poor and became rich, and he built a mansion. Sesame pressers worked nearby, and when they pressed the seeds his mansion shook. He came to Rav Ashi, who told him that when they studied in Rav Kahana's study hall they used to say Rabbi Yosei concedes in the case of a person's own arrows.
08.why: The mishna has Rabbi Yosei saying each neighbor may use his own land as he likes; Rav Ashi reports that even Rabbi Yosei agrees when one's activity directly strikes a neighbor, and this case shows that principle being applied.

people.name: Pappei Yona'a
people.about: A once-poor man who grew rich, built a mansion, and complained that his neighbors' sesame pressing shook it.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage Pappei Yona'a came to with his complaint.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: An earlier Sage whose view Rav Ashi applies to the case.

terms.meaning: A phrase for damage that shoots out directly from a person's own activity onto a neighbor's property, like an arrow he has fired.

09.note: Rava bar Rav Hanan had palm trees along the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard. Birds roosted in the palms and came down to damage the vines, so Rav Yosef told him to cut the trees down. Rava bar Rav Hanan said he had kept the required distance; Rav Yosef answered that a greater distance is needed between trees and vines. Rava bar Rav Hanan said he himself would not cut them, quoting Rav that it is forbidden to cut down a palm that yields a kav of fruit, and Rabbi Hanina that his son Shikhhat died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time. If Rav Yosef wished, he said, he could cut them himself.
09.why: The mishna discusses how far trees must be planted from a neighbor's field; this case tests whether the standard distance is enough when trees stand beside a vineyard.

people.name: Rava bar Rav Hanan
people.about: Owner of palm trees on the border of Rav Yosef's vineyard, who refuses to cut them down himself.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Owner of the vineyard damaged by birds roosting in his neighbor's palms.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage quoted as saying his son Shikhhat died for cutting down a fig tree before its time.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume, a few liters; a palm yielding this much fruit is still productive.
The core law code of the early Sages, on which the Gemara comments.

10.note: Rav Pappa had palm trees along the border of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua's land, and found Rav Huna digging and cutting their roots. Rav Huna cited the mishna that a man may dig three handbreadths to clear roots for his plow; when Rav Pappa said he was digging deeper, Rav Huna said he was digging cisterns, ditches and caves, where the mishna lets him cut downward. Rav Pappa said he tried every argument without success until he quoted Rav Yehuda that a strip the public has long used may not be ruined. After Rav Pappa left, Rav Huna said to himself he should have answered that this rule applies only within sixteen cubits of the tree, and he was cutting beyond that.
10.why: The mishna has just ruled that a landowner may cut a neighbor's roots that spread into his field; this exchange tests how far that right goes.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Owner of palm trees whose roots his neighbor was cutting.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Rav Pappa's neighbor, who was digging on his own land and cutting the roots.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose ruling about land long used by the public finally persuades Rav Huna.

terms.meaning: A measure of about the width of a hand, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters.
A measure from elbow to fingertip, roughly half a meter.
The core law code of the early Sages, on which the Gemara comments.

11.note: Rami bar Hama and Rav Ukva bar Hama bought a maidservant together. One used her in the first, third and fifth years, the other in the second, fourth and sixth. Then someone came forward claiming she belonged to him. They came before Rava, who told them they had done this so that neither could establish a claim of ownership against the other; and just as their use gave them no such claim against each other, it gave them none against anyone else.
11.why: The Gemara is discussing whether a presumption of ownership requires continuous use over three years; this case shows that use split into alternating years does not count.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: One of two Sages who bought a maidservant together and took turns using her year by year.

people.name: Rav Ukva bar Hama
people.about: The other partner in buying the maidservant.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who judged the case when an outsider claimed the maidservant.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

12.note: A man found someone living in his house and asked what he was doing there. The occupant said he had bought it from him and lived in it for the years needed to establish ownership. The man said he had been away in distant settlements, so he could not have protested. They came before Rav Nahman, who told the occupant to go and prove that he had lived there those years. Rava objected: is that the law? The one who seeks to take something from another must bring the proof.
12.why: The Gemara is discussing what counts as a three-year presumption of ownership; this case asks who must prove the occupation when the owner says he was away, and the Gemara then notes that Rava and Rav Nahman rule the opposite way in another case.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who told the occupant to prove his years of use.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects that the burden of proof belongs on the claimant.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.
The rule that whoever wants to take property from someone else must bring the evidence.

13.note: A man found another working his land and asked what he was doing there. The occupant said he had bought it from a third person and used it for the years needed to establish ownership. The man replied that the seller was a robber who had stolen the field. The occupant said he had witnesses that he had first consulted the man, who told him to go ahead and buy. The man explained that he had said so because the occupant was easier to deal with than the robber. Rava said the claimant had stated the law correctly.
13.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of disputed land; it goes on to ask whether Rava's ruling follows Admon, who accepts the same reasoning even when the claimant signed the bill of sale, and answers that a casual remark is weaker than a signature.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who accepted the original owner's explanation.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

14.note: Two land disputes are told. In the first, a man found someone on his land; the occupant said he bought it from a third person and had used it the required years. The man said the seller was a robber. The occupant said he had witnesses that the man came to him at night and asked to buy it. The man said he had wanted to buy his way out of a lawsuit, and Rava said people do pay to avoid litigation. In the second, the occupant again said he bought the land and used it the required years; the claimant said he held a deed showing he had bought it from that same seller four years earlier. The occupant said by 'the required years' he meant many years, not just three, and Rava said people commonly speak that way.
14.why: The Gemara is gathering Rava's rulings on contested land; these cases show which explanations of seemingly damaging behavior or words he accepted, and the Gemara then adds that the second ruling holds only if the occupant's use began before the claimant's deed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules in both disputes.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

14.flag: The STORY combines two separate land cases (segment 4 and segments 5-6) that are not one narrative.

15.note: Two men disputed a piece of land, each saying it had belonged to his ancestors. One brought witnesses that it had been his ancestors' land; the other brought witnesses that he had used it for the years needed to establish ownership. Rabba said the occupant should win, since he could have said he bought it from the claimant and been believed. Abaye answered that this argument does not hold when witnesses contradict him. The occupant then said: yes, it was your ancestors', but I bought it from you, and when I said it was my ancestors' I meant I relied on it as if it were.
15.why: The occupant's change of story leads the Gemara to ask whether a litigant may state a claim and then revise it; Ulla says he may and the Sages of Neharde'a say he may not.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who would award the land to the occupant.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rabba because witnesses contradict the occupant.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.
A legal argument: a person is believed if he could have won with a stronger claim had he wanted to lie.

16.note: Two men disputed a piece of land, each saying it had belonged to his ancestors. The first brought witnesses that it had been his ancestors' land and that he had used it for the years needed to establish ownership; the second brought witnesses only that he had used it for those years. Rav Nahman said the two testimonies about use cancel each other out, leaving the testimony about the ancestors, so the land goes to the first man. Rava objected that this testimony had been contradicted. Rav Nahman began to answer that although it was contradicted about the use of the land, and here the text breaks off.
16.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a litigant may revise his claim; it now turns to contradictory witnesses, and next asks whether Rav Nahman and Rava differ as Rav Huna and Rav Hisda do over witnesses who contradict each other.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who awards the land to the man with witnesses about his ancestors.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects that this testimony was contradicted.

terms.meaning: In this law, someone who uses property openly for three straight years, with no protest from the owner, is presumed to have bought it, even without a deed.

16.flag: The STORY ends mid-sentence; Rav Nahman's reply to Rava is completed in the next segment.

17.note: The case continues: the second man, who at first had witnesses only to his use of the land, then brought witnesses that it had belonged to his own ancestors. Rav Nahman said: we put the first man on the land and we can take him off it, and we are not worried about contempt of court. Rava, or some say Rabbi Zeira, objected from a teaching about a woman whose divorce or husband's death is disputed by two pairs of witnesses: if she remarried before contrary witnesses came, Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Yosei says she need not leave. Rav Nahman said he had meant to act, but since Rava and also Rav Hamnuna in Syria had raised this objection, he would not. Then he went out and did act. Onlookers thought he had made a mistake, but the Gemara says he relied on great authorities.
17.why: The Gemara is asking whether a court that has ruled may reverse itself on new testimony; it goes on to show that this depends on a dispute among early Sages about restoring a priest's status, which is the 'great authorities' Rav Nahman relied on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who first gave the land to one man and then took it back after new witnesses came.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who objects to reversing the ruling; some say it was Rabbi Zeira.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who raised the same objection to Rav Nahman in Syria.

people.name: Rabbi Menahem son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: An early Sage whose teaching about a remarried woman is quoted against Rav Nahman.

terms.meaning: The worry that a court which changes its rulings will look unreliable and lose respect.
A teaching from the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the core law code, but quoted in the Gemara.

18.note: A man found another on his land and asked what he was doing there. The occupant said he had bought it from him and showed a bill of sale. The man said the bill was forged. The occupant leaned over and whispered to Rabba: yes, it is forged, but I had a proper bill of sale and lost it, so I thought I would hold on to this one at least. The ruling is not given in this part of the text.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge to whom the occupant whispered his confession about the forged bill.

terms.meaning: A written document recording that land was sold, used as proof of ownership.

18.flag: The STORY stops before Rabba's and Rav Yosef's rulings, which fall in the AFTER segments.

19.note: A man demanded a hundred dinars from another and showed a promissory note. The other said the note was forged. The first man leaned over and whispered to Rava: yes, it is forged, but I had a proper note and lost it, so I thought I would hold on to this one at least. The ruling is not given in this part of the text.
19.why: The Gemara has just told the same situation with a forged bill of sale for land; it brings this parallel case about money and then gives the final ruling, which treats land and money differently.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge to whom the lender whispered his confession about the forged note.

terms.meaning: A written document recording a loan, which a lender can use to collect the debt.
A coin; one hundred dinars was a sizable sum.

19.flag: The STORY stops before the rulings on it, which fall in the AFTER segments.

20.note: A rumor spread that Rava bar Sharshom was living off land that belonged to orphans. Abaye asked him what had actually happened. He explained that he had held the land as collateral from the orphans' father, who also owed him other money, and had used it for the agreed years. He reasoned that if he gave it back and then claimed the other debt he would have to take an oath, so he planned to hide the collateral document and keep using the land until the debt was paid, since he could have claimed he bought it and been believed. Abaye told him he could not claim he bought it, because everyone knew it was orphans' land. He told him to return it, and to take them to court when they grew up.
20.why: The Gemara has just ruled that money stays where it is when a claim rests on weak grounds; this case tests the 'he could have made a stronger claim' argument, and Abaye rejects it because the land was publicly known to be the orphans'.

people.name: Rava bar Sharshom
people.about: A Sage rumored to be living off orphans' land, which he had held as collateral from their father.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who questions Rava bar Sharshom and tells him to return the land.

terms.meaning: Property a borrower hands over to a lender as security; here the lender could use the land and its produce for a set number of years.
A solemn sworn statement in court; the Sages required one from anyone collecting a debt from orphans' property.
